The prisma update in the catch block (lines ~190-198) is not wrapped in its own try/catch. If it throws, the error escapes the for loop and the remaining reminders are skipped.
The code uses reminder.retryCount + 1 from a value read earlier (lines 184 and 195) instead of { increment: 1 }. Overlapping cron runs can lose increments.

safe_urlopen sits outside the try block, so a network error propagates as a 500. get_user_info is also unguarded.

Restart in flusher.py:206 only kills when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process), which doesn't match SpawnProcess or threads, so a hung worker keeps running while a replacement starts on the same shards.

The processes are created with the spawn context (SpawnProcess subclasses BaseProcess, not multiprocessing.Process), so the isinstance guard skips kill(). The old code called kill() unconditionally, so this is a regression.
join() breaks at flusher.py:337 once the deadline passes and never terminates the remaining processes. terminate() is also behind the same non-matching isinstance check.
_create_process_for_shard (flusher.py:127) has no callers in src. The old process may also survive a restart because of the isinstance issue.

The docstring says one process per shard, but the CLI option defaults to 1 (consumers/__init__.py:433) and the constructor caps at max_processes, so all shards share one process by default. The off-by-one part of the title is dubious, but the docstring/default mismatch is real.
The test patches time.sleep with a no-op via monkeypatch, so the added time.sleep(0.1) waits for nothing and the test stays racy.
The test only asserts the total shard count (4) and the process count. It doesn't check the per-process distribution or exercise any flushing.

slots.ts:~140 computes `end` from slotStartTime identically to `start`, working hours are compared in UTC rather than organizer timezone, and the find callback returns true for any out-of-range block of that day.
Two separate dayjs objects compared with === can never be equal, so the zero-length override branch is dead code.
The override branches only reject slots that end at or before the override start or start after its end, so a slot overrunning the override end is not rejected.

The specific claim that later overrides are never considered is wrong: Array.find keeps iterating when the callback returns undefined (slots.ts:103-125). The remaining busy-skip problem is covered by f4.
`if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` runs before the busy.every check, so busy times and bookings on override days are ignored.
TimeRange.timeZone is optional (packages/types/schedule.d.ts:5), and packages/lib/slots.ts:212 passes it to .tz() without a fallback.

The matcher in getSchedule.test.ts only checks the actual slots against the expected list by index, so fewer slots than expected would still pass; the new test therefore only weakly guards timezone shifts. The title's claim of a contradicting comment is overstated.

scheduleEmailReminders.ts:43-51 cron cancels every cancelled reminder with scheduledDate <= now+1h, before it sends; the deleteMany at lines 31-38 only removes reminders whose scheduledDate has already passed, so they were already sent.

With immediateDelete the function cancels the SendGrid batch and returns (emailReminderManager.ts) without deleting the WorkflowReminder row, and the old DELETE of the scheduled send is removed; for reschedules the row stays.
The findMany has no method filter, and the single try/catch around the loop stops on the first failed SendGrid request. Deletes are lazy Prisma promises that only run at the final Promise.all.

Reminders removed by the earlier deleteMany (scheduledDate <= now, scheduleEmailReminders.ts:31-38) have already been sent. The 1-hour cron window (line 47) cancels the rest before their send time, so the claimed gap does not exist.

handleCancelBooking.ts calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder without await. They now do DB writes that were previously awaited via prismaPromises, so the writes may be dropped when the serverless handler returns.

The reminders come from remindersFromStep, queried by workflowStepId of the user's own workflow (workflows.tsx ~line 505), so ownership is already implied. The race and ownership concerns are speculative.

getOriginalRescheduledBooking is the only place originalRescheduledBooking is assigned (handleNewBooking.ts:779) and it includes workflowReminders (line 772). The delete functions catch their own errors (smsReminderManager.ts:187, emailReminderManager.ts try/catch), so none escape.

The diff changes the cleanup ticker in cleanup.go from 10 minutes to 1 minute, with no related need in this change.
The added r.log.Error calls in the time-based cleanup log every batch with the full ID list and condition at Error level.
The count-based cleanup adds the same Error-level per-batch log with all IDs, and err is always nil at that point because the preceding check returned on error.
The orphaned-tag cleanup adds an Error-level log with IDs on every iteration.
The check compares the configured batch size, not len(ids), so the ID-inlining path is taken needlessly when batch size is over 999 and the actual ID count is smaller.
The loop rebuilds the string with Sprintf for every ID, which is O(n^2) for batches of up to tens of thousands of IDs.
In the diff, t.Cleanup is registered after createTestAnnotations and the require-based count assertions, so a failure there skips the cleanup and can leave rows behind.

pkg/infra/tracing/tracing.go:91-96 registers a contextual log provider that adds traceID from the context, and ConcreteLogger.FromContext (pkg/infra/log/log.go:203-210) applies it, so traceID is still logged.
tagDeviceUI (impl.go ~line 80) sets the local cache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice, so after a limit rejection the next request within the cache window returns nil at the cache check and passes.
client.go now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request ctx, so the DB count and write sit on the auth path, and the goroutine's panic recovery is gone.
CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices and then the upsert as separate statements with no transaction or lock, so concurrent new devices can exceed the limit.

updateDevice's BETWEEN filter applies to the stored updated_at column, so it is meaningful. A device older than 30 days is outside CountDevices' window too, so treating it as new and reporting the limit is consistent.

A property typed undefined is assignable to the interface type number | undefined (packages/grafana-data/src/types/config.ts:200), so there is no type conflict. The 0-versus-undefined point is trivial.

In dualwriter_mode3.go the Storage Create and Update error paths call recordLegacyDuration, so storage failures are recorded in the legacy metric.
The Legacy.DeleteCollection goroutine in dualwriter_mode3.go reports its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration.

queue_consumer.py:90 breaks at the first offset missing from all_offsets, so any real gap in delivered offsets (e.g. compaction or transaction markers) stops commits.
mark_committed prunes all_offsets and line 86 restarts the scan at last_committed+1, so if the next delivered offset is higher the loop breaks immediately and nothing is committed again.
The worker loop at queue_consumer.py:129 checks self.shutdown, which pool.shutdown sets at line 234, so workers can exit with items still queued. Nothing handles rebalance or revocation.
The repo targets Python 3.13: .python-version is 3.13.1 and pyproject.toml:47 sets python_version = "3.13". queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown exist there.

The queues and workers are in-memory per process (queue_consumer.py:~185-200), so the salted hash is stable for the life of the process, and queued state is lost on restart anyway. The finding itself concedes it is fine within one process.

list(dict.keys()) under the GIL does not raise on concurrent insert, and lock creation uses the atomic setdefault (queue_consumer.py:~49). Per-key reads and writes happen under the partition lock (lines 55-80).

The queues are unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize), so there is no backpressure. The worker's finally block calls complete_offset even when processing raised, so failed items still become committable, contradicting the docstring.

The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` contradicts the docstring about not blocking commits. It checks nothing useful about committing past an error, and can fail if the 1s commit loop fires.
The test asserts 20 str keys cover all 3 queues using Python's salted hash(), which is nondeterministic across runs. The chance of a miss is small (about 0.1%) but nonzero.
After Lock() at webassets.go:50 the cache is not re-checked, so concurrent cold-cache callers each re-read the manifest serially.

In non-dev mode a non-nil cache returns early at webassets.go:44-46, so the assignment at line 74 can only replace nil with nil; a valid cached value is never reset, and a cached nil just triggers a re-read.

readWebAssets returns a nil dto whenever err is non-nil (webassets.go:~104-125), so readWebAssetsFromCDN never gives a non-nil result with an error. The file fallback at line 62 runs whenever the CDN read fails, so no partial result is cached and no nil dereference occurs.
enableSqlExpressions in pkg/expr/reader.go returns false on both paths (the `if enabled` branch and the fall-through), so the flag has no effect.
The check always fails, so ReadQuery returns 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, which is misleading.

All DB stub methods in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return 'not implemented'. parser.go:26 calls RunCommands via the package-level TablesList, and sql_command.go:100 calls QueryFramesInto. DB.TablesList itself has no callers.

service.go:116-121 returns deny from permDenialCache before any permission lookup and service.go:153 sets it for the 30s shortCacheTTL. Nothing deletes the entry when permissions change, so a new grant stays denied until the entry expires.

cache.go:30-32 joins uid, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping, and the key shares the userPermCacheKey prefix. Names or folder UIDs containing '_' can make different tuples produce the same key. Practical impact is small.

The key at service.go:116 is built the same way on every request. A different raw ID form only produces a separate cache entry, never a wrong decision. Anonymous users all get the same Viewer-role permissions (getAnonymousPermissions), so sharing a denial key is correct.

The fallback at service.go:147 runs the same checkPermission with the same folder lookups, so an error from the cached-permissions check would recur there. Returning early at service.go:127-130 is equivalent. getCachedIdentityPermissions errors are deliberately treated as a cache miss that falls through to the DB.

Counting a miss when cached permissions do not allow is accurate, because the DB fallback is needed to catch an outdated cache. After that one DB fetch, service.go:153-155 writes the denial cache, so repeated denials are served from cache.

The server now does the cache lookup itself, which makes the in-process client cache redundant. getIdentityPermissions is called only from Check (service.go:139) and List (service.go:186), and both consult getCachedIdentityPermissions first (service.go:123, 180). No cache-less path reaches the DB more often.

service_test.go TestService_getUserPermissions has no remaining case with cacheHit true, so the cacheHit field and its branches are dead. The 'should return error if store fails' case (nil permissions, no error field) expects an empty map, so it never tests an error.
server.go:258-262 returns nil, err after s.Init fails without calling s.cancel(), so the cancelable context created earlier is leaked.
bleve.go BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu during the build; only the map write at line 137 is locked, and getOrCreateIndex/build in search.go has no other serialization for the same key.
TotalDocs at bleve.go:144-146 ranges over b.cache without taking cacheMu, while BuildIndex writes the map under the lock, so it is a real unsynchronized read.
search.go:216 calls TotalDocs after the event goroutine has started, and handleEvent can reach getOrCreateIndex and write the cache concurrently with the unlocked read.
Stop sets initErr (server.go:321,339), but the handlers no longer call Init, so that gating is gone and requests are served after Stop.
The diff adds an unconditional postgres skip to the test, so that path loses coverage; the skip is marked TODO.

The empty-expr filter at querySplitting.ts:297 runs before interpolation, and the shard path passes already-interpolated queries into this map, so filters and interpolation are applied again.
The test asserts toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5), which encodes the double interpolation (1 call in runShardSplitQuery plus 4 in runSplitQuery) and depends on shard grouping.

ECDSAAlgorithmTest uses a default P-256 key pair for ES384 and ES512 and only asserts an encode/decode round trip, with no known vectors.

verifySafeHtml throws RuntimeException when the derived English file can't be opened, instead of reporting a message.

Matches are consumed in order and earlier tags are removed, so replaceFirst removes the current tag. A mismatch adds a message and leaves the tag for the sanitizer, which then flags the difference (VerifyMessageProperties.java ~L104-116).
HTML_TAGS is lowercase-only, so an uppercase tag in the English source would not enable the HTML policy.

The English value contains '<div>', so the SOME_HTML policy applies and strips the disallowed div. VerifyMessagePropertiesTest.java:37-39 asserts the 'Illegal HTML' message is produced, so the fixture does exercise the disallowed-element path.

With a null strategy, UpgradeLogicFactory.java:36-39 returns RecreateOnImageChangeUpgradeLogic, which only compares images (RecreateOnImageChangeUpgradeLogic.java:46-53) and never calls update-compatibility, so ROLLING_UPDATES isn't needed.

The test base deployment sets no feature spec (the only FeatureSpec use in the operator tests, apart from CRSerializationTest, is UpgradeTest.java:112-115), so nothing is overwritten, and the test never mutates the list.

The macro is used only for update-compatibility, and that command exits with FEATURE_DISABLED when the feature is off (UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java:46). Appending --features=rolling-updates is intended, and the macro callers pass only subcommand arguments.

CompatibilityResult.java:34-35 does change the recreate exit code from 4 to 3 and assigns 4 to FEATURE_DISABLED, which is a real behaviour change, even though docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc:128-133 already describes 3 and 4 that way.

The CAUTION sits in the update-strategies section and the operator only fails when update-compatibility is run with the feature disabled, which the null-strategy path never does (UpgradeLogicFactory.java:36-39); the wording is imprecise but not a real defect.
The reader thread is started with new Thread(...).start() and never joined, so an in-flight read exception can be added after assertThat runs and the thread can outlive the test.
The reader loop has no pacing and only ends when deletedAll is set; if a remove() throws, deletedAll.set(true) is never reached and the thread spins forever.

The only caller, GroupUtils.java:90, passes the value to setSubGroupCount(Long) (GroupRepresentation.java:94), which accepts null, so nothing unboxes it; the null return is the intended fix for a deleted group.
Admin events are cleared per test by AbstractEventsSupplier.java:40, and polling starts from the test start time (AbstractEvents.java:40), so unpolled delete events do not leak into later tests.
The added cleanup lines call identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, but every IDP the test creates is aliased "idp-alias-N", so none are cleaned up.

getLoginPredicate() now also requires an org-linked IDP to have BROKER_PUBLIC=true, but the getForLogin javadoc (lines 151-152) lists only enabled, not link-only and not hidden. IdentityProviderBean.java:226 also uses this predicate, so its semantics change.
GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource, so a view-only admin passes the global manage check.

AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup names resources by group id, but getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes groupResource.getId() (the resource UUID) to hasPermission and adds that UUID to the result set.

MgmtPermissions.java:335 evaluates a single ResourcePermission for the requested resource, so the returned permissions can only concern that resource and the missing resourceId comparison has no effect.

AdminPermissionsSchema.java:107 switches on resourceType, which throws NullPointerException when it is null. The old code reached the descriptive IllegalStateException. The update path in RepresentationToModel.java:1423 doesn't visibly validate resourceType first.

The V1 gate is what keeps V2-only deployments from calling ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, which throws UnsupportedOperationException (ClientPermissionsV2.java:~171). V2 has no cleanup implementation to skip, so the finding's own argument shows the gate is deliberate.

AdminPermissionsSchema.init (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:222-252) creates a type resource named after each type, including 'Clients', when the admin-permissions server is created. hasPermission also returns early on a null server and on a different realm, so the type resource is non-null on this path.

findByType(CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) also returns the generic 'Clients' type resource, whose name is the type (AdminPermissionsSchema.java:~246). If that resource is granted, 'Clients' is added as a client id, and all-clients grants are not expanded to individual clients.

The claim that this differs from V1 is wrong. V1 ClientPermissions.canMapRoles (ClientPermissions.java:536-556) also only evaluates the map-roles scope and does not fall back to canManage. Treating map-roles as a separate scope is the same design.

The findByName argument order is correct: ResourceStore.findByName(server, name, ownerId) at ResourceStore.java:154. The default two-argument form passes resourceServer.getClientId() as the owner, which is the same server identity as server.getId(). The vague canView(ClientScopeModel) complaint is not a concrete defect.

org.junit.Assert.fail throws AssertionError, which is an Error and not caught by catch (Exception). The try/catch tests in PermissionClientTest therefore still detect a missing exception. Mixing JUnit4's fail with JUnit5 is only a style issue.

The requireNonNull for rawTokenId checks grantType, so a null rawTokenId passes the constructor.

Throwing on malformed IDs is deliberate and tested (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest expects a RuntimeException for bad IDs). Legacy IDs without a colon are handled gracefully at DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:76-77, and the only callers of getTokenContextFromTokenId are tests.

An unset grant type falls back to UNKNOWN ('na') at DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:59-61. 'na' is registered in both maps at DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit, so encodeTokenId does not throw. The grant-type attribute values come from registered grant type provider IDs.

Context.setFormParams has no callers in services (grep found none), and the only Context is built at TokenEndpoint.java:149. A missing grant_type yields null, which falls back to 'na' at DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.java:59-61 instead of failing.

The attribute lives in the ClientSessionContext attribute map, which is separate from request form parameters. A grep of services and server-spi-private found no other use of the 'grant_type' key as a context attribute, so no collision exists.
